definition: In this historical source, social contagion is treated as a type of mimetic process in which one mind is influenced by another through imitative copying. It refers to the spread of expressions or reactions by repetition, often in a relatively impulsive, echoing way.

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record Mimetism; pinned source text

reasons: The packet does not explicitly define “social contagion” as “one mind is influenced by another”; it mentions “states of consciousness” associated with “circular (or repeating) reaction,” but not a direct mind-to-mind influence formulation.

The packet does not explicitly state that it refers to the “spread of expressions or reactions by repetition”; while it does describe “circular (or repeating) reaction” and “more or less slavish and impulsive copying,” it does not define social contagion specifically as a spread mechanism of expressions/reactions.

The definition’s phrasing (“often in a relatively impulsive, echoing way”) is only partially supported: the packet supports “slavish and impulsive copying” and “repeating,” but it does not use or clearly warrant the “echoing” formulation.
